items.text: Representations of a diagonalisable group $G=D(M)$
$\operatorname{Dist}(G)=k^M$ (functions on $M$, ordinary product); the diagonal maps into the completed tensor product $k^M\hat\otimes k^M$ and involves the law of $M$.
$V$ a $k$-module. A representation of $G$ on $V$ = a continuous $k^M$-module structure on $V$ (each $u\mapsto ux$ factors through a finite quotient). Projectors in $k^M$:
p_m=\text{Dirac distribution at } m;\qquad p_m^2=p_m,\quad p_mp_{m'}=0\ (m\ne m'),\quad \sum_mp_m=1\ \ (\text{product topology})
Continuity: for each $x\in V$, $p_mx=0$ except for finitely many $m$, and $\sum_mp_mx=x$.
V=\bigoplus_{m\in M}V_m\qquad(\text{a grading of type }M)
\chi_m\colon G\to\mathbb G_m\quad(\text{character attached to }m),\qquad g\in G(k'),\ x\in V_m\otimes k'\ \Longrightarrow\ gx=\chi_m(g)\,x
The category of representations of $G=D(M)$ on $k$-modules is equivalent to the category of $M$-graded $k$-modules. The law of $M$ enters only in the tensor product:
V_m\otimes V'_{m'}\ \text{has degree}\ m+m',\qquad \chi_m\chi_{m'}=\chi_{m+m'}
Same over any scheme $S$ (quasi-coherent modules): $D(M)$ is defined over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$.
The constant group scheme $M_S$

$M_S$ = sum of $|M|$ copies of $S$ (exact: commutes with finite limits and products, so group objects go to group objects). Affine over $S$ iff $M$ finite or $S$ empty; not of finite type if $M$ is infinite.
D(M)=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\text{gr}}(M_S,\mathbb G_{m,S})\colon S'\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{S'\text{-gr}}(M_{S'},\mathbb G_{m,S'})
\operatorname{Hom}_{S'}(M_{S'},X)=\operatorname{Map}\bigl(M,\,\Gamma(S',X)\bigr);\qquad\text{with laws: homomorphisms }M\to\Gamma(S',X)
\operatorname{Hom}_{\text{gr}}(M_{S'},\mathbb G_m)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\text{gr}}\bigl(M,\Gamma(S',\mathcal O_{S'})^{*}\bigr)
Biduality of the constant group
M_S\longrightarrow D(D(M))=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\bigl(D(M),\mathbb G_m\bigr)\quad\text{is an isomorphism}

It says: a homomorphism $G\to\mathbb G_m$ comes from a section of $M_S$ over $S$ = a locally constant function $S\to M$ = a partition $S=\coprod_mS_m$ into open sets; from a unique $m\in M$ if $S$ is connected and non-empty.

Proof. $\mathbb G_m=\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}_{\mathcal O_S}(\mathcal O_S)$: a homomorphism $G\to\mathbb G_m$ = an operation of $G$ on the free module $\mathcal O_S$ of rank one = a grading $\mathcal O_S=\bigoplus_m(\mathcal O_S)_m$.
p_m\in\Gamma(S,\mathcal O_S)\ \text{mutually orthogonal projectors},\ \sum_mp_m=1\ \Longleftrightarrow\ S=\coprod_mS_m\ \text{(open)},\ \ p_m=1\text{ on }S_m,\ 0\text{ elsewhere}
So $M_S$ is reflexive for $\mathbb G_m$, and so is $D(M)$: duality $D$ is an anti-equivalence between constant commutative groups and diagonalisable groups.

Duality with values in $\mathbb G_m$ governs commutative group schemes (reflexive: affine ones, constant ones); extends to abelian varieties with $\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1(G,\mathbb G_m)$ = the dual abelian variety.
Cartier duality

$G$ commutative monoid, finite and locally free over $S$: $G=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal A$, $\mathcal A=f_*\mathcal O_G$ a quasi-coherent sheaf of algebras, locally free of finite type as an $\mathcal O_S$-module.
Dual (for monoids replace $\mathbb G_m$ by $\mathcal O^{\times}$ = $\mathcal O$ with its multiplication; $\mathbb G_m$ is the largest group subobject):
D(G)=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\text{monoid}}\bigl(G,\mathcal O^{\times}\bigr)
G\longrightarrow D(D(G))\quad\text{an isomorphism (Cartier duality)}
Claim: $D(G)$ is representable, by a finite locally free scheme of monoids.
A monoid homomorphism $G_{S'}\to\mathcal O^{\times}_{S'}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_{S'}[t]$ = an algebra homomorphism $\mathcal O_{S'}[t]\to\mathcal A_{S'}$ = a section $u$ of $\mathcal A_{S'}$:
D(G)\subset W(\mathcal A),\qquad D(G)(S')\subset\Gamma(S',\mathcal A_{S'})
Conditions on $u$ (unit to unit, multiplicative), with $\pi\colon\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ and augmentation $\varepsilon\colon\mathcal A\to\mathcal O_S$:
\varepsilon(u)=1,\qquad \pi(u)=u\otimes u
$W(\mathcal A)$ is representable (the vector bundle of $\mathcal A^\vee$); these equations define a closed subfunctor.
